title: Bilateral hypopyon in syphilitic uveitis
journal: American Journal of Ophthalmology Case Reports
case_prompt:
A 38-year-old Hispanic man presented with a 2-day history of bilateral progressive visual loss, conjunctival hyperemia, and photophobia, beginning in the right eye and involving the left eye within one day. Medical history included uncontrolled hypertension and bacterial pharyngitis treated with oral antibiotics two weeks before ocular symptoms. He denied recent sexual activity but reported past intercourse with both male and female partners. He smoked tobacco and drank alcohol socially. Review of systems was notable for general malaise, frontal headaches, sore throat, arthralgias, right-sided testicular pain, lower back pain worsened by exercise, easy bruising, alopecia, perineal hypopigmentation, a scaly rash on palms and soles, and nail changes but was otherwise unremarkable.
On examination, visual acuity was finger counting at 3 feet in the right eye and 20/40 in the left eye; intraocular pressures were normal. Pupils were equal and reactive without afferent defect. Slit-lamp examination showed bilateral conjunctival injection, non-granulomatous keratic precipitates, 4+ anterior chamber cells, and a hypopyon. Funduscopic examination revealed 4+ vitritis in the right eye and 3+ vitritis in the left eye. B-scan ultrasonography demonstrated bilateral vitreous opacities without choroidal masses or retinal detachment. Extraocular examination showed moth-eaten alopecia; glossal leukoplakia with erythematous maculae on the hard palate; erythematous macular lesions on both palms; onychodystrophy, onycholysis, and longitudinal nail striae; psoriasiform plaques on the plantar surfaces; and hypopigmented patches on scrotal and perianal skin. Vertebral tenderness at L4–S1 and bilateral sacroiliac pain on FABER testing were noted; neurologic examination was normal.
Empiric treatment included bilateral intravitreal vancomycin, ceftazidime, voriconazole, hourly topical prednisolone acetate 1%, atropine sulfate 1%, oral indomethacin, and intravenous acyclovir. After three days with persistently poor fundus view, a diagnostic and therapeutic pars plana vitrectomy was performed in the right eye. Intraoperatively, severe vitritis with multiple preretinal precipitates was observed. Cytologic analysis of vitreous fluid showed no malignant cells and revealed a mixed acute and chronic inflammatory infiltrate.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Infectious endophthalmitis — “As the differential diagnosis of bilateral hypopyon with severe vitritis includes infectious endophthalmitis, a bilateral vitreous tap, and injection of vancomycin, ceftazidime, and voriconazole was done.”
2. Fungal endophthalmitis — “…helped us rule out (and potentially treat) a fungal infection, which is known to represent approximately one-fifth of positive endophthalmitis isolates in Puerto Rico.”
3. Malignancy — “Cytopathologic findings were negative for malignant cells.”
4. Behçet’s disease — “The patient denied … oral or genital ulcers.”
5. HLA-B27-associated uveitis — “Testing for HLA-B27 haplotype … was negative.”
